differential: Nephrotic syndrome
Periorbital edema in a young child is a classic presentation, typically due to minimal change disease at this age.
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Can cause periorbital edema and facial swelling in pediatric patients following streptococcal infection.
Allergic reaction
Periorbital edema can result from environmental allergens, food allergies, or contact allergens affecting the periorbital area.
Angioedema
Can present with periorbital swelling in children, either hereditary or acquired, often episodic in nature.
Orbital/periorbital cellulitis
Infection can cause periorbital swelling, though typically accompanied by erythema and other inflammatory signs.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out any diagnoses.

differential: Minimal change disease (nephrotic syndrome)
Most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in preschool-aged children presenting with periorbital and lower extremity edema without fever or hypertension.
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Can present with edema in children, though the absence of hypertension and hematuria makes this less typical.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Can cause nephrotic syndrome in children with generalized edema, though less common than minimal change disease in this age group.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Important cause of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children presenting with significant proteinuria and edema.
IgA nephropathy (Henoch-Schönlein purpura nephritis)
Can present with edema in children, though typically accompanied by other systemic manifestations like rash or joint pain.
eliminated: Allergic reaction
Absence of urticaria, pruritus, respiratory symptoms, and the 4-day duration with progressive lower extremity involvement makes this unlikely.
Congestive heart failure
Normal temperature and lack of other cardiac findings (tachypnea, hepatomegaly, jugular venous distension) make this less likely, though tachycardia is present.

differential: Minimal change disease
Classic presentation with nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria >3.5g/day equivalent, hypoalbuminemia, edema) and fatty casts in a preschool-aged child with normal complement levels.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Can present identically to minimal change disease with nephrotic syndrome but is less common as initial presentation in this age group.
Membranous nephropathy
Presents with nephrotic syndrome and normal complement levels, though rare in young children and more typical in adults.
Congenital nephrotic syndrome
Could cause severe nephrotic syndrome at young age, though typically presents earlier in infancy or first year of life.
IgA nephropathy
Can occasionally present with heavy proteinuria and nephrotic features, though typically shows hematuria which is absent here.
eliminated: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Normal complement levels rule this out (typically shows low C3).
Lupus nephritis
Normal complement levels and absence of systemic features make this unlikely.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Normal complement levels argue against this diagnosis (typically shows low C3 and/or C4).
Acute tubular necrosis
Normal creatinine and no clinical history of nephrotoxic insult or hypoperfusion.

differential: Minimal change disease
Renal biopsy confirmed diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, which is pathognomonic for this diagnosis.
Secondary minimal change disease (medication/malignancy-induced)
While biopsy shows minimal change disease pattern, secondary causes should be considered though less likely in a 4-year-old.
Early focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Can present identically to minimal change disease clinically and may show only podocyte effacement on initial biopsy before sclerotic lesions develop.
IgM nephropathy
May show podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy but would require immunofluorescence showing mesangial IgM deposition to distinguish from minimal change disease.
C1q nephropathy
Rare entity that can mimic minimal change disease histologically but requires immunofluorescence showing dominant C1q staining, which was not reported.
eliminated: Membranous nephropathy
Electron microscopy would show subepithelial immune deposits and basement membrane spikes, not isolated podocyte effacement.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Normal complement levels and absence of hematuria make this unlikely, plus biopsy is inconsistent.
IgA nephropathy
Would show hematuria and mesangial IgA deposits on immunofluorescence, not isolated podocyte effacement.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Would show basement membrane duplication and low complement levels, inconsistent with biopsy findings.
Acute tubular necrosis
No clinical history of hypotension or nephrotoxin exposure, and biopsy findings are inconsistent.

differential: Nephrotic syndrome
Periorbital edema in a young child is a classic presentation, especially if bilateral and worse in the morning.
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Can cause periorbital edema due to fluid retention from glomerular inflammation in pediatric patients.
Allergic reaction
Periorbital swelling can result from environmental allergens, food allergies, or contact allergens.
Periorbital cellulitis
Bacterial infection of periorbital tissues can cause localized swelling around the eyes in children.
Hypothyroidism
Can present with periorbital edema and myxedema, though less common in this age group.

differential: Minimal change disease (nephrotic syndrome)
Periorbital and lower extremity edema in a young child is classic for nephrotic syndrome, most commonly due to minimal change disease in this age group.
Post-infectious glomerulonephritis
The rash combined with edema suggests a possible immune-mediated glomerulonephritis following a recent infection (e.g., streptococcal).
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)
Maculopapular rash on trunk with edema could represent HSP, though typical purpuric distribution on lower extremities is not explicitly described.
Acute rheumatic fever
The combination of rash and systemic findings including tachycardia could suggest rheumatic fever, though edema is less typical.
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Though uncommon at age 4, SLE can present with nephrotic syndrome, rash, and systemic manifestations.
eliminated: Angioedema
The presence of pitting edema and duration of 4 days makes this unlikely; angioedema is typically non-pitting and transient.

differential: Minimal change disease
Classic nephrotic syndrome presentation in a young child with massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and normal complement levels without hematuria.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Can present identically to minimal change disease but may show more resistance to therapy and less common as initial presentation in this age group.
Membranous nephropathy
Presents with nephrotic syndrome and normal complements, though less common in young children and typically lacks the associated rash.
IgA nephropathy
Can cause proteinuria and edema, though typically presents with hematuria which is absent here, making it less likely.
Systemic lupus erythematosus
The combination of nephrotic syndrome, rash, and thrombocytosis could suggest lupus nephritis, but normal complement levels make this unlikely.
eliminated: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Absent hematuria and normal complement levels rule out this diagnosis.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)
Lack of hematuria and the distribution/type of rash are inconsistent with this diagnosis.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Normal complement levels effectively exclude this diagnosis.
Acute postinfectious glomerulonephritis
Nephritic features (hematuria, hypertension) are absent and complements are normal.

differential: Minimal change disease
Renal biopsy confirms diffuse podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, which is pathognomonic for this diagnosis.
NSAID-induced minimal change disease
The maculopapular rash raises concern for drug reaction, and NSAIDs are a known cause of minimal change disease with associated hypersensitivity features.
Hodgkin lymphoma-associated minimal change disease
Though rare in young children, Hodgkin lymphoma can present with minimal change disease and constitutional symptoms including rash.
Acute interstitial nephritis with concurrent minimal change disease
The rash and minimal change disease pattern could suggest an immune-mediated process affecting both tubules and glomeruli.
Idiopathic minimal change disease with viral exanthem
The most common presentation of minimal change disease in children, with the rash representing an incidental viral infection.
eliminated: Membranous nephropathy
Renal biopsy shows foot process effacement without immune complex deposition characteristic of membranous nephropathy.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Normal complement levels and absence of hematuria make this unlikely, and biopsy is inconsistent.
IgA nephropathy
Biopsy shows minimal change disease without mesangial IgA deposits, and presentation lacks hematuria.
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis
Electron microscopy shows diffuse (not focal) foot process effacement without sclerosis.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Normal complement levels and biopsy findings rule this out.
